title: The Sleeping Sickness Mystery: Why Did Thousands Suddenly Fall Asleep?
summary: Imagine feeling so tired you couldn't stay awake for days. Not just a nap—we're talking weeks of sleeping! That's what happened to thousands of people around 1920. Doctors called it "sleeping sickness," or encephalitis lethargica. It was super weird. Some people slept all the time. Others couldn't sit still and ran around like they had endless energy. A doctor named Constantin von Economo first wrote about it in 1917. He said patients got headaches and felt yucky, then fell into a deep sleep. They could be woken up, but sometimes they'd act wild and confused. About half of those who survived were never the same—their personalities changed completely. The sickness killed around 500,000 people. At the same time, a huge flu pandemic was sweeping the world. Some scientists thought the flu caused the sleeping sickness. But the sleeping sickness lasted ten years longer than the flu, and studies of old brains didn't find the flu virus. In 2012, researchers guessed it might be an enterovirus, a kind of virus that can make muscles weak. Others think the body's own defenses attacked the brain by mistake. The last known survivor, Philip Leather, died in 2002 after spending most of his life unable to move in a hospital. Today, the disease is super rare—only 80 cases in 85 years. But because we don't know what caused it, scientists worry: could it suddenly return? It's a spooky medical mystery that's still unsolved.
why_it_matters: A sickness from the past that we don't fully understand could teach scientists how to stop new brain diseases, so solving this mystery could protect people in the future.

background_read: In 1918, a terrible flu pandemic (often called the Spanish flu) sickened about one-third of all people on Earth. Around the same time, encephalitis lethargica appeared, confusing doctors because it wasn't the same as the flu. Dr. Constantin von Economo (a brain doctor in Vienna, Austria) first recorded the strange symptoms in 1917. Some scientists think the body’s immune system, after fighting a virus, may accidentally damage the brain—a pattern seen in other diseases like multiple sclerosis. Philip Leather lived most of his life in a hospital unable to move, until his death in 2002. Today, studying this old mystery helps doctors understand similar brain-immune reactions.
Article_Structure: WHO: Dr. Constantin von Economo (the first to describe the illness) and the thousands of patients who fell into deep sleep or had endless energy.
WHAT: A mysterious disease called encephalitis lethargica that caused weeks of sleeping, personality changes, and often death.
WHERE: It appeared globally, but first cases were noted in Europe during World War I.
WHY: Doctors still don't know what caused it, and the article warns that without an answer it could return.

perspectives.description: The disease pushed scientists to study how viruses and the immune system can affect the brain, leading to discoveries that help with modern conditions.
For the victims and their loved ones, the illness was terrifying—it stole people's personalities and left many trapped in their bodies.
Since the cause remains unknown, there is a small chance a similar outbreak could happen again, so experts keep watching for mysterious brain illnesses.
